questions.scenario: A service reports 95% line coverage. Code review finds that many tests call methods without any assertions.
questions.question: What does the coverage figure actually tell you?
options: That mutation testing is unnecessary
That 95% of the code is correct
Which code was executed by tests, not whether the tests would detect a bug in it
That only 5% of bugs remain
questions.explanation: Coverage measures execution. Assertion-free tests execute code without checking results; mutation testing reveals how many faults the tests would catch.

questions.scenario: PIT reports: 'changed conditional boundary: amount > 5000 → amount >= 5000 — SURVIVED' in the fee calculator.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Exclude the fee calculator from mutation testing
Increase the JaCoCo threshold
Add a test at exactly ₦5,000.00 that asserts the correct fee, so the mutant is killed
Change the code to >= so the mutant matches
questions.explanation: A surviving boundary mutant means no test distinguishes > from >=. A test exactly on the boundary closes the gap.

questions.scenario: A team adds JaCoCo with an 80% threshold on the whole codebase of a 10-year-old service at 35% coverage. Every build now fails and developers want to remove the check.
questions.question: What is a more workable approach?
options: Exclude all legacy packages permanently
Write assertion-free tests to raise the number quickly
Apply the threshold to new and changed code (for example via a SonarQube quality gate on new code) and raise the overall bar gradually
Remove coverage checks entirely
questions.explanation: Gating new code improves quality as the code is touched without blocking all work; gaming or removing the metric helps no one.

questions.scenario: SonarQube marks a line that builds a CORS configuration as a security hotspot.
questions.question: What is the correct handling?
options: A developer reviews it; if the configuration is safe (specific trusted origins), mark it reviewed with a written justification
Mark it as a false positive without looking
Delete the CORS configuration
Ignore hotspots because they are not bugs
questions.explanation: Hotspots are security-sensitive code that needs human judgement. Reviewing and documenting the decision is what a quality gate expects.

questions.scenario: You are defining a quality gate for pull requests.
questions.question: Which conditions are sensible? (Choose two.)
options: Coverage on new code of at least 80%
At least 100 commits per week
Total lines of code below 10,000
No new bugs or vulnerabilities above minor severity
questions.explanation: Gates should measure the quality of what is being changed. Code size and commit counts say nothing about correctness or risk.

questions.scenario: The architecture rule is that domain classes must never depend on web or persistence classes. A new developer imports a controller DTO into a domain service.
questions.question: Which tool can enforce this rule automatically in the unit-test phase?
options: PIT
ArchUnit, with a rule that classes in ..domain.. must not depend on classes in ..web..
JaCoCo
Docker
questions.explanation: ArchUnit expresses architecture constraints as tests that fail the build when dependencies cross forbidden boundaries.

questions.scenario: SonarQube flags a rule as a 'bug': amount.equals(BigDecimal.ZERO) is used to check for a zero balance.
questions.question: Why is this flagged, and what is the fix?
options: BigDecimal cannot be compared; convert to double
Use == instead of equals
BigDecimal.equals also compares scale, so 0.00 is not equal to 0; use compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) == 0 or signum() == 0
It is a false positive; equals is always correct
questions.explanation: A balance of 0.00 would not equal BigDecimal.ZERO with equals, so the check silently fails. compareTo or signum compares numeric value only.
